title: [Green Development Performance Evaluation and Differentiation Improvement Strategy in the Yangtze River Delta Region: Based on the Synergistic Perspective of Carbon Reduction， Pollution Reduction， and Green Expansion].
abstract: Green development is a key strategy to promote the modernization of our ecological and environmental governance system and realize the comprehensive transformation of the economy and society. Based on the input-output framework， a green development performance evaluation system is constructed from the perspective of carbon reduction， pollution reduction， and green growth synergy， and the green development performance of 27 cities in the Yangtze River Delta Region from 2012 to 2023 is measured by using the super-efficient SBM model. The spatio-temporal evolution law is also analyzed by combining kernel density estimation and the Dagum Gini coefficient decomposition method. The results show that： ① During the study period， the overall green development performance of the Yangtze River Delta Region showed a trend of "first decreasing and then rising，" with the average fluctuating from 0.598 to 0.877， an increase of 46.66%. ② At the provincial level， Zhejiang and Anhui had obvious performance advantages at the beginning of the study period， but the improvement rate was slow， while the green development performance of Shanghai and Jiangsu increased significantly during the study period. At the city level， the green development level of six cities including Shaoxing and Chizhou has always been at the forefront of efficiency， with Wuxi， Changzhou， Suzhou， Jiaxing， and other cities increasing the most， while the green development performance of Tongling and Wuhu in Anhui has declined. ③ The intercity differences in green development performance in the Yangtze River Delta Region eased during the study period， and the overall Gini coefficient decreased from 0.248 to 0.125， of which intra-provincial differences were the main source of the overall differences. Based on the empirical results， a four-quadrant diagram is constructed from the two dimensions of economic development level and green development performance； the differentiated paths for performance improvement in different cities are proposed； and a green collaborative guarantee mechanism is proposed from the aspects of policy coordination， industrial collaboration， ecological joint governance， and science and technology sharing.

title: Naxos disease: current insights from early clinical observations to genetics and precision medicine.
abstract: Naxos disease is the prototype of the Naxos disease cardiocutaneous spectrum, a group of inherited desmosomal disorders characterised by distinctive hair and skin abnormalities that precede the development of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM). Since its original clinical description in 1986 and the subsequent identification of the first ACM-causing gene (JUP), Naxos disease has provided fundamental insights into the pathogenesis, diagnosis and management of inherited desmosomal cardiomyopathies. This review provides current insights into the evolving clinical spectrum, encompassing the characteristic cutaneous signature, early electrical abnormalities, progressive structural myocardial remodelling, inflammatory ("hot-phase") episodes, ventricular arrhythmias and heart failure. We discuss the expanding genotype-phenotype relationships involving JUP, DSP and DSC2, highlighting how distinct genetic substrates influence ventricular involvement, disease severity and clinical outcomes while sharing common desmosomal mechanisms. Particular emphasis is placed on early clinical recognition, multimodality imaging, genetic diagnosis, risk stratification and lifelong multidisciplinary management. Finally, we discuss the emerging role of international collaborative registries, including NAXCARE, in generating prospective real-world evidence to refine genotype-informed surveillance, improve risk prediction and support precision medicine. Nearly four decades after its original description, Naxos disease has evolved from a rare inherited syndrome into the prototype of desmosomal cardiomyopathy, demonstrating how careful clinical observation can drive molecular discovery, precision medicine and improved patient care.

title: Zfpm1 regulates endothelial-mesenchymal transition and endocardial cell differentiation.
abstract: The endocardium is the endothelial component of the heart that forms valves. Endocardial (EC) cells undergo endothelial-mesenchymal transition (EndoMT) which distinguishes them from endothelial (ET) cells, despite sharing markers and a mesodermal origin. Nfatc1, uniquely labels EC cells but is not sufficient for EC cell specification, since knockouts form valves, albeit underdeveloped, therefore the regulators that specify EC fate remain incompletely defined. Using an in vivo Nfatc1 reporter system, we show that EC and ET cells are transcriptionally distinct and identify the transcription factor Zfpm1 (Fog1), as a potential regulator of EC cell specification. In an in vitro embryonic stem cell differentiation model, Zfpm1 knockdown results in an impaired EC cell differentiation, with reduced endothelial-mesenchymal transition and altered contractility and beating phenotype, consistent with reduced differentiation of EC cells affecting the crosstalk with myocardial cells. These findings are consistent with data linking mutations in the human ZFPM1 gene with non-syndromic tetralogy of Fallot. This and the broad expression pattern across all regions of the cardiac outflow tract support a role for Zfpm1 in mammalian EC cell differentiation and endothelial-mesenchymal transition. This study extends the in vivo evidence of its relevance to cardiac development and provides new insights into the transcriptional control of EC lineages.

title: Machine learning in placental research: a review and guide for future studies.
abstract: Machine learning approaches are increasingly applied across biomedical research to analyze complex, high-dimensional datasets and identify patterns that may inform disease diagnosis and biological discovery. In reproductive and placental research, these methods are used to investigate fetal development, pregnancy complications, and early-life health outcomes using molecular and clinical data. Machine learning approaches have widely been applied to placental and obstetric imaging, such as ultrasound, although these applications have been extensively reviewed elsewhere. Despite growing interest, many placental machine learning studies face recurring methodological challenges that limit interpretability and translational relevance. In this review, we summarize common machine learning approaches and concepts relevant to applying machine learning to placental biology. We then examine emerging applications of machine learning in placental research across genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics. We propose best practices for designing robust and reproducible machine learning studies in placental research and highlight future directions, emphasizing prospective prediction and data sharing to support clinically meaningful translation.

title: Building Block-Based Molecular Networking Enables Targeted Isolation of PTP1B-Inhibitory Triterpene-Flavanol Conjugates from the Stems of Tripterygium regelii.
abstract: Celastrol, a quinone methide triterpenoid present in plants of the genus Tripterygium, is a potent leptin sensitizer and a promising scaffold for anti-obesity drug development. Metabolite profiling of the stems of Tripterygium regelii using UPLC-qTOF-MS/MS, combined with building block-based molecular networking (BBMN) analysis, led to the isolation of ten previously undescribed triterpene-flavanol conjugates (1-10), including celastrol derivatives, as well as the annotation of 34 additional congeners sharing a similar core scaffold. The structures of compounds 1-10 were elucidated through comprehensive spectroscopic analyses, chemical derivatization, and quantum chemical calculations. All isolates exhibited configurationally stable sp3-sp2 axial chirality at ambient temperature, and both P- and M-configured atropisomers were identified. In vitro evaluation of protein tyrosine phosphatase 1B (PTP1B) inhibition revealed that compound 10 exhibited potent activity, with an IC50 value of 0.6 ± 0.1 μM, acting as a mixed-type inhibitor. These triterpene-flavanol conjugates represent a new structural class with potential as lead compounds for the development of anti-obesity agents.

title: Jestvirus, a Novel Genus in the Family Autotranscriptaviridae Infecting Aeromonas.
abstract: Aeromonas species are ubiquitous, aquatic, opportunistic pathogens; however, their viral predators remain underexplored. Here, we isolated and characterized Aeromonas phage vB_AsaP_JS1, a dsDNA phage with a short non-contractile tail that infects Aeromonas salmonicida. Comparative analyses indicate that vB_AsaP_JS1 diverges from representative T7-like phages, with gene content similarity below 50% and a maximum amino acid identity of 70% or less. It forms a supported monophyletic clade in both phylogenomic and protein-based trees. Gene-sharing network analysis further shows that vB_AsaP_JS1 and its closest relatives form a distinct, isolated cluster, clearly separated from all currently recognized genera within the family Autotranscriptaviridae and related lineages of Caudoviricetes. Collectively, these features satisfy ICTV criteria for genus demarcation and support the establishment of a novel phage genus, tentatively designated Jestvirus. Functional annotation highlights a compact transcriptional module containing a single-subunit T7-like RNA polymerase and a streamlined replication packaging operon. Several putative host-interaction-related genes, including a deoxycytidine kinase homolog, a PelC-like protein, and a putative glycosidase, are encoded in the genome; their possible roles in nucleotide scavenging or host interaction during infection represent hypotheses that require experimental validation. Metagenomic read mapping reveals sequence-level signals related to vB_AsaP_JS1 in wastewater datasets from multiple geographic regions, suggesting a potentially wider environmental distribution for this phage lineage than previously recognized, though confirmation of phage identity and prevalence will require further investigation. Together, our results expand the known genomic diversity of T7-like phages and provide taxonomic, functional, and ecological evidence for a new phage lineage within Caudoviricetes.

title: Loss of protein function resulting in severe phenotypes of X-linked myotubular myopathy caused by novel synonymous and splice-site variants in the MTM1 gene.
abstract: X-linked myotubular myopathy (XLMTM) is a severe, often neonatally lethal congenital neuromuscular disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the MTM1 gene. Affected neonates typically present with profound hypotonia, generalized muscle weakness, and respiratory insufficiency requiring immediate ventilatory support at birth. Splice-site variants in MTM1 account for approximately 20% of molecularly confirmed cases of XLMTM. Two male neonates with molecularly confirmed severe XLMTM, born at distinct gestational ages, were enrolled. Next-generation sequencing followed by validation with Sanger sequencing identified a de novo synonymous variant (c.183A > G) in MTM1 in Patient 1 and a canonical splice-site variant (c.444+1G > A) in Patient 2. The functional impact of these variants was assessed via longitudinal clinical assessments, skeletal muscle biopsy with histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses, and minigene splicing assays. Minigene assays confirmed pathogenic exon skipping for both variants, with the c.183A > G variant causing complete skipping of exon 4 in Patient 1 and the c.444+1G > A variant causing complete skipping of exon 6 in Patient 2. Both events resulted in frameshifts and the subsequent loss of myotubularin protein expression. Despite sharing severe, life-threatening clinical and histopathological features, including neonatal-onset respiratory failure, centrally located myonuclei, reduced myofiber diameter, and rapid disease progression, the two patients displayed markedly divergent respiratory trajectories. These findings indicate that the novel synonymous variant c.183A > G and the splice-site variant c.444+1G > A in MTM1 can cause comparable lethal phenotypes via pathogenic mechanisms mediated by exon skipping.

title: [Current Systems and Challenges in Acute Ischemic Stroke].
abstract: The devices and techniques used in mechanical thrombectomy have reached a high level of maturity. Over the next decade, the focus will shift from an era of developing treatments and technologies, to one of delivering treatments in a sustainable manner. Key challenges include workforce development, the establishment of healthcare systems to reduce regional disparities in access to care, reimbursement reform and healthcare economics, and physician work-style reform through task shifting and task sharing to allied healthcare professionals. As these issues are closely interconnected, comprehensive policy and system reforms that address them in an integrated manner are urgently required.

title: Neurology and headache medicine in Malawi: territory, education, and the path to strengthening primary care in sub-Saharan Africa.
abstract: Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) bears a disproportionate burden of neurological and pain-related diseases while facing a severe shortage of trained specialists. In this context, expanding neurology and, particularly, headache medicine, through education and integration within primary care represents both a necessity and an opportunity. This Perspective proposes a context-sensitive framework in which three interconnected domains-territory, culture, and capacity-shape the accessibility, acceptability, and sustainability of neurological care. Drawing on the experience of the International Headache Society (IHS)-DREAM healthcare network partnership in Malawi, we examine how locally adapted education, task-shifting and task-sharing can contribute to capacity building while highlighting the limitations of approaches that focus on training alone. We argue that closing the neurological treatment gap requires a shift from specialist-centred to system-centred neurology, integrating workforce development with primary care, culturally grounded community engagement, appropriate supervision and referral pathways, supportive national health policies, and equitable access to essential medicines. Task shifting and task sharing between physicians and non-physician clinicians may constitute a sustainable component of this model when appropriately regulated, supervised, remunerated, and integrated with specialist support and referral pathways. Rather than proposing a model for direct transfer across SSA, this Perspective advocates locally led, context-dependent implementation strategies capable of adapting to diverse health systems. Such an approach reframes global neurological capacity building from the episodic transfer of expertise towards the development of resilient and sustainable systems of care.

title: Transcription Factor TabZIP12 Orchestrates the ABA Signaling Pathway to Regulate Drought Tolerance in Wheat (Triticum aestivum L.).
abstract: Drought-induced osmotic stress severely compromises crop yield productivity and threatens global food security. This study reports TabZIP12, a wheat bZIP transcription factor, in regulating osmotic stress tolerance. Under drought and abscisic acid (ABA) treatment, TabZIP12 expression was significantly upregulated with a dose- and time-dependent manner. Y-2H, BiFC, Co-IP, and In vitro pull-down assays confirmed a physical interaction between TabZIP12 and the kinase TaSnRK2.6. This kinase further interacted with the phosphatase TaPP2C50, which in turn interacted with the ABA receptor TaPYL1. These interactions suggest the TabZIP12-involved constitution of a synergistic signaling module (TaPYL1-TaPP2C50-TaSnRK2.6-TabZIP12). Transgene analyses revealed the essential functions of the signaling module members. Of which, TaPYL1, TaSnRK2.6, and TabZIP12 positively while TaPP2C50 negatively regulated drought tolerance, due to their roles in modulating key physiological processes associated with stomatal movement, osmolyte biosynthesis, root morphology, ABA biosynthesis, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging. TabZIP12 possessed an ability in binding with the promoters of critical stress-responsive genes, namely SLAC1 gene TaSLAC1-4, P5CS gene TaP5CS1, PIN-FORMed gene TaPIN3, NCED gene TaNCED3, and APX gene TaAPX6 and activated their activation. Transgenic validation confirmed these genes in positively modulating drought adaptation. Notably, in a wheat variety panel sharing contrasting drought response, the transcripts of TabZIP12 and its target genes correlated significantly with plant dry matter and yield under drought conditions. Haplotype analysis identified TabZIP12-Hap1 as a favorable allele associated with enhanced drought tolerance. Our findings elucidate novel mechanisms underlying the bZIP-mediated drought response and provide valuable genetic resources for breeding drought-resistant wheat varieties.

title: Implementation of Programmatic Mailed Fecal Immunochemical Testing for Colorectal Cancer Screening in the Veterans Health Administration.
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic prompted the Veterans Health Administration (VA) to implement programmatic mailed fecal immunochemical test (FIT) screening for colorectal cancer. This paper describes VA's programmatic mailed FIT development, implementation and initial outcomes. VA adapted mailed FIT processes from a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention-sponsored Mailed FIT Implementation Guide, performed regional pilots, created a national Mailed FIT Implementation Team (MFIT), and issued formal policy. The MFIT then provided training and disseminated tools to support VA mailed FIT programs. Programmatic mailed FIT has been implemented in 89.5% of eligible facilities. Between December 1, 2022 and September 30, 2025, 643,933 FIT were ordered and 40.2% were returned. Of those, 89.1% were testable and 10.9% were cancelled, primarily due to missing sample collection date (63.2%) or receipt >15 days after collection (31.5%). Of the 230,427 FIT results, 7.4% were abnormal and colonoscopy was completed in 54.4%. Among 5846 VA colonoscopies, adenomas were detected in 68.0%, and adenocarcinoma was found in 2.3%. Linear regression analysis demonstrated a direct correlation between increasing mailed FIT adoption and the proportion of Veterans who are up to date with screening (r=0.65, p=0.003). VA has successfully developed and disseminated strong practices for population-level CRC screening outreach with programmatic mailed FIT. This practice is associated with moderate levels of adherence and significant improvements in the overall proportion of Veterans who are up to date with screening. Further dissemination of mailed FIT programs, process improvement, and sharing of best practices is ongoing.

title: The wisdom of the diverse crowd(funders)
abstract: Crowdfunding platforms aim to democratize entrepreneurial finance by creating ecosystems that elicit the ‘wisdom of crowds’—aggregating the judgments of individual and often amateur funders. However, there is limited evidence on whether crowds can effectively apply their collective wisdom on these platforms. Our study addresses these questions by analyzing a crowdlending platform that connects Western lenders with borrowers in developing countries. We examine whether lenders effectively screen borrowers, identify platform attributes that influence lenders’ screening accuracy, and uncover the underlying mechanisms driving these effects. To achieve this, we exploit interventions by platform administrators that allow us to observe the counterfactual repayment performance of loans that failed to attract sufficient funding. Our results indicate that rowdlenders can effectively screen creditworthy borrowers, but only when financial information about borrowers is made available. Lenders’ screening effectiveness diminishes substantially for prosocial loans, as many funders converge on similar, socially motivated decisions. These findings provide novel evidence on crowdlenders' performance, highlighting key trade-offs for crowdfunding platforms and offering actionable insights for their administrators.

title: DETERMINING FACTORS OF INTENTION TO PAY ZAKAT VIA FINANCIAL TECHNOLOGY (FINTECH)
abstract: This study aims to examine muzakki’s intention to utilize Financial Technology (Fintech) platforms for paying zakat by investigating the behavioral and psychological determinants. The research integrates the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), with a particular emphasis on prosocial motivations and perceived risk factors. This study uniquely expanded the view of perceived risk variables, including psychological, legal, and time risks, by integrating altruism and empathy as prosocial constructs into a single framework. The research employs a quantitative approach, utilizing a structured questionnaire distributed to 150 purposively selected respondents. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares-Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to test the relationships between the variables. The findings reveal that perceived altruism and empathy significantly influence muzakki’s intention to adopt fintech for zakat contributions. In contrast, perceived risk—which encompasses aspects such as privacy, legality, time, psychological burden, and security—does not have a significant effect on the intention to use fintech for zakat. These results suggest that emotional and social motivations are stronger predictors of digital zakat payment adoption than perceived risk. Therefore, zakat institutions and fintech developers are advised to focus on building trust and emphasizing the altruistic and empathetic values of zakat in their platforms, as this effort is expected to strengthen the development of a sharia-compliant digital financial ecosystem and contribute to achieving social goals, such as poverty alleviation and reducing inequality.

title: The Life-sustenance Hypothesis: Understanding Human-Nature Connection by Integrating Rousseau's Philosophy to Contemporary Systems Biological Viewpoints
abstract: This paper develops the life-sustenance hypothesis to explain the multifaceted phenomenon of the human-nature connection. It is based on an interpretation of Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s philosophy brought into contemporary times via recent multidisciplinary research and theoretical underpinnings. Rousseau suggested that humans have two innate, instinctive drives he called amour-de-soi and pitié—a self-preservative drive, and its enlargement, an inclination to help other living beings in distress. The life-sustenance hypothesis is rooted in a systems biological framework situating humans as interconnected parts within a nested system of life. Corresponding to Rousseau’s drives, this interconnectedness is suggested to give rise to the dynamics between two life-preserving orientations that guide our manners-of-being in the world: a self-sustaining and a ‘life-sustaining’ orientation shared by all organisms, albeit manifested differently. The experience of nature connectedness, along with altruistic impulses, are proposed to be human manifestations of the life-sustaining orientation. Moreover, in line with Rousseau’s philosophy, it is posited that the modern, individualistic lifestyle has given rise to an imbalance between these orientations leading to problems in prosociality, proenvironmentalism, and overall well-being. One means by which to regain balanced manners-of-being might be to enhance our nature connectedness. Possible physiological indicators for the hypothesis are explored.

title: The Moving Mandala: Exploring the Pro-Social Effects of Musical and Non-Musical Synchrony in Children in a Virtual World.
abstract: Synchronous movement between individuals has been shown to increase pro-sociality, such as closeness and generosity. To date, synchrony research tests these effects using a variety of movement tasks, including musical and non-musical coordination. However, musical versus non-musical synchrony may have separable pro-social effects. To test this, we had 60 children immersed in an augmented reality space called the 'Moving Mandala' where they moved asynchronously with only visual cues, synchronously with only visual cues or synchronously with musical and visual cues. We then tested for differences in pro-social effects using sharing and proxemics tasks. Results showed that while the synchrony version of the mandala led to greater closeness in the proxemics task, the musical synchrony led to more pro-sociality on the sharing task. The implications of these findings are discussed.

title: The effect of psilocybin on empathy and prosocial behavior: a proposed mechanism for enduring antidepressant effects
abstract: Psilocybin is a serotonergic psychedelic shown to have enduring antidepressant effects. Currently, the mechanism for its enduring effects is not well understood. Empathy and prosocial behavior may be important for understanding the therapeutic benefit of psilocybin. In this article we review the effect of psilocybin on empathy and prosocial behavior. Moreover, we propose that psilocybin may induce a positive feedback loop involving empathy and prosocial behavior which helps explain the observed, enduring antidepressant effects.

title: Drivers of cooperation in social dilemmas on higher‐order networks
abstract: Understanding cooperation in social dilemmas requires models that capture the complexity of real-world interactions. While network frameworks have provided valuable insights to model the evolution of cooperation, they are unable to encode group interactions properly. Here, we introduce a general higher-order networks framework for multi-player games on structured populations. Our model considers multi-dimensional strategies, based on the observation that social behaviours are affected by the size of the group interaction. We investigate the dynamical and structural coupling between different orders of interactions, revealing the crucial role of nested multi-level interactions and showing how such features can enhance cooperation beyond the limit of traditional models with uni-dimensional strategies. Our work identifies the key drivers promoting cooperative behaviour commonly observed in real-world group social dilemmas.

title: Agent-based simulation of equity-oriented water reallocation under drought: A case study of the Geum River Basin
abstract: Study region : Geum River Basin, South Korea, a structurally heterogeneous watershed with 14 agricultural, 12 domestic/industrial intake, and 3 hydropower stakeholders. The basin has the highest agricultural water demand among South Korea’s six major river basins, with precipitation concentrated in the summer monsoon season, making dam operations critical for balancing competing water demands during irrigation. Study focus : This study develops an integrated framework to improve equitable water allocation during droughts by coupling a basin-scale allocation model with an Agent-Based Model (ABM). While centralized optimization overlooks decentralized social dynamics, autonomous stakeholder agents make voluntary diversion decisions based on locally perceived reliability deficits, redistributing water to the most vulnerable peers via hypothetical conveyance infrastructure. Streamflow is represented by SWAT-derived daily inflows spanning 39 water years (October 1981–September 2020). New hydrological insights and conclusions : First, agricultural water supply vulnerability in the Geum River Basin is governed less by absolute demand magnitude and more by basin topology and infrastructure configuration. Tributary-dominated subbasins (Agr 7, Agr 11, and Agr 13), which are structurally isolated from the regulated mainstem, exhibited the lowest supply reliability during the severe historical droughts of 1994–1997 and 2014–2017, identifying these locations as priority targets for adaptive drought management in the basin. Second, agent-based simulation of voluntary water donation among Geum River stakeholders demonstrates that equity improvements can emerge as system-level outcomes from repeated decentralized interactions. During drought period, the agricultural Gini coefficient decreased from 0.152 (no ABM) to 0.097–0.117 across three behavioral scenarios, with the largest reliability gains concentrated at the most structurally vulnerable tributary nodes. Third, sensitivity analysis across nine supply–demand combinations confirmed that the simulated equity benefit within the Geum River Basin is robust to variations in inflow magnitude and irrigation demand scaling, with gains increasing proportionally under higher demand pressure. However, the Pro-social scenario yielded diminishing equity returns relative to the Bounded Rational scenario, as excessively frequent donations reduced the reliability of intake donor stakeholders, suggesting that moderate rather than maximum cooperation produces the most balanced outcomes across stakeholder types.

title: Resolving social dilemmas with minimal reward transfer
abstract: Abstract Social dilemmas present a significant challenge in multi-agent cooperation because individuals are incentivised to behave in ways that undermine socially optimal outcomes. Consequently, self-interested agents often avoid collective behaviour. In response, we formalise social dilemmas and introduce a novel metric, the general self-interest level, to quantify the disparity between individual and group rationality in such scenarios. This metric represents the maximum proportion of their individual rewards that agents can retain while ensuring that a social welfare optimum becomes a dominant strategy. Our approach diverges from traditional concepts of altruism, instead focusing on strategic reward redistribution. By transferring rewards among agents in a manner that aligns individual and group incentives, rational agents will maximise collective welfare while pursuing their own interests. We provide an algorithm to compute efficient transfer structures for an arbitrary number of agents, and introduce novel multi-player social dilemma games to illustrate the effectiveness of our method. This work provides both a descriptive tool for analysing social dilemmas and a prescriptive solution for resolving them via efficient reward transfer contracts. Applications include mechanism design, where we can assess the impact on collaborative behaviour of modifications to models of environments.

title: Influences of music and rhythm on prosocial behavior in preschool children
abstract: Music has existed in human culture for at least 40,000 years and is present today in all societies. Its perception, appreciation and production are based on a set of cognitive abilities commonly referred to as "musicality." Some authors have suggested that musicality may have an evolutionary origin. Specifically, it may have evolved because music promotes social cohesion within groups. This hypothesis is supported by studies in developmental psychology, which show that joint music-making promotes empathy in 8 to 11-year-olds, as well as cooperation and helping behavior in 4-year-old children. However, many questions remain unanswered, particularly regarding the effects of music listening on social behavior (beyond joint production), the conditions under which such effects may be observed (e.g., individual versus joint listening), the musical properties and mechanisms involved (e.g., the role of rhythm and interpersonal synchronization), and the broader evolution of musicality across the living world beyond our own species. In 2017, we already demonstrated a positive influence of joint listening to classical music on social interaction in a cooperative task context in children aged 3 to 6, as well as in a parrot species, the cockatiels (suggesting convergent evolution in humans and certain birds, thus indicating a partly biological, not just cultural, origin of musicality). The study presented here focuses specifically on children but is also part of a larger comparative project involving humans, non-human primates, and birds. In the case of children, this study showed that percussive, rhythmic electronic music fostered more social interactions and cooperation among pairs of 3 to 6-year-old children compared to classical music (Mozart's Sonata K448), white noise, a "scrambled" version of the stimulus used, or silence. The role of rhythm and interpersonal synchronization will be further explored in the future by testing the influence of new stimuli listened to together or separately, with or without concurrent music production. We also plan to examine the spontaneous movements of individuals during listening and their relationship to observed behaviors in subsequent prosocial tasks.

title: Is leisure‐time reading related to empathy and social skills in 8‐ to 10‐year‐old children?
abstract: There is growing interest in the effects of reading on empathy and prosocial behaviour but not enough is known about the associations among these variables in children. In a study undertaken at a single time point, we examined children's leisure reading and self-reported prosocial behaviour, and whether the relation between them was mediated by affective or cognitive empathy or by theory of mind. We tested 113 English-speaking children aged 8-10 years from a UK primary school. Analyses showed that reading and prosocial behaviour are related, and that the relation was partly explained by variance shared with empathy, particularly affective rather than cognitive empathy. Future work focusing on causal aspects of these relations should provide further guidance on the practical implications of these results.

title: MOOD AND EMPATHY ON PROSOCIAL BEHAVIOUR AMONG MUSLIM ADOLESCENTS IN PADANG CITY
abstract: This research is motivated by the phenomenon at the Dharmabakti Nusantara Health Vocational School in Padang City; mood and empathy are thought to influence prosocial behaviour. This study aims to analyse: 1) mood, empathy and prosocial behaviour, 2) the relationship between mood and prosocial behaviour, 3) the relationship between empathy and prosocial behaviour, and 4) the relationship between mood and empathy together with prosocial behaviour. The method used in this study is a Quantitative method that aims to determine the relationship and influence between variables. The research sample was taken from the existing population of 80 students. The research instrument used a questionnaire with a Likert scale model. The data were analysed with descriptive statistics, simple regression, and multiple regression; the results of the research data analysis obtained an R-value of 0.558 with a p level = 0.000 (p <0.05). There is a significant relationship between mood and empathy with prosocial behaviour. R2 =0,311 %. This study proves a positive and meaningful relationship between philosophy and heart in prosocial behaviour at SMK Dharmabakti Nusantara Pota Padang.

title: The Relationship between Well-Being, Empathy, Moral Identity, and Spirituality on Prosocial Behavior among Malaysian Youth
abstract: This study explores the influence of well-being, empathy, moral identity, and spirituality on prosocial behavior among Malaysian youth.A quantitative approach was employed with a sample of 411 participants, using Pearson correlation and multiple regression analyses to investigate the relationships between these variables.The results revealed that moral identity was the strongest predictor of prosocial behavior, followed closely by spirituality, empathy, and well-being.These findings highlight the central role of moral identity in shaping prosocial actions, with spirituality and empathy also playing significant roles.Well-being, while slightly less influential, still contributes meaningfully to prosocial behavior by promoting emotional stability and life satisfaction.The study emphasizes the importance of fostering moral development, spiritual growth, and emotional well-being to encourage prosocial behavior in youth.Policymakers, educators, and community leaders are encouraged to implement programs that focus on these key areas to promote a more compassionate and engaged youth population.

title: Severity over source: Understanding transgressors' motive attributions of punishment
abstract: Punishment conveys social information to transgressors, who attribute motives to punishers. Drawing on the motive-attribution framework, we examined whether transgressors' attributions to competitive (i.e. harming transgressors), individualistic (i.e. managing one's own interests) and prosocial (i.e. healing relationships) motives differ depending on whether punishment is administered by victims (second-party punishment) or uninvolved observers (third-party punishment), and how these attributions relate to downstream affective, relational and behavioural outcomes. In an incentivized Stealing Game, participants could steal valuable points and were punished either by the victim or an observer. Subsequently, transgressors reported their motive attributions, affect and willingness to reconcile and completed a measure of prosocial behaviour towards an unrelated other. Contrary to predictions, motive attributions did not systematically differ between second- and third-party punishment, except that third-party punishment was more strongly attributed to reputational concerns (i.e. a subdimension of individualistic motive attribution). Punishment severity emerged as an important predictor, with harsher sanctions linked to stronger competitive and individualistic attributions. Competitive motive attribution, in turn, was associated with higher negative affect and lower positive affect, willingness to reconcile and prosocial behaviour. Overall, transgressors' responses to punishment were less clearly shaped by who punished and more closely linked to punishment severity and motive attribution.

title: The Role of the Effectiveness of Mosque Social Activities and Their Consistency in Repetition Donation Decisions (Case Study of Masjid Raya Al Insan)
abstract: Mosques play a vital role in Islam, serving not only as places of worship but also as centers for various social activities and economic empowerment, including the collection of social funds such as zakat, infaq, and sadaqah (charity). However, data from the 2024 Mosque Information System (SIMAS) of the Ministry of Religious Affairs of the Republic of Indonesia shows that of the total 694,725 mosques and prayer rooms, only 28,138 have a Mosque Welfare Agency (BKM), indicating that the majority of mosque management remains traditional and has not adopted modern management. Masjid Raya Al Insan (MRAI) in Kebayoran Lama, South Jakarta, is known for frequently holding social and humanitarian activities, both routine and incidental, for the congregation and the community living around the mosque. Previous research has examined factors such as transparency, accountability, the attitude of mosque management, and the social and religious influences of donors on trust and donation decisions. However, there is still little research that specifically examines the role of the effectiveness of mosque social activities and their consistency on repeat donation decisions. Using a qualitative case study method through in-depth interviews with administrators and donors, this study evaluates the role of the effectiveness and consistency of MRAI's social programs on repeat donations. The results show that the effectiveness of social activities is assessed by the emotional impact and tangible solutions for the community, not simply by statistical figures. It was found that repeat donation decisions are driven by a strong synergy between theological motivation and trust in the integrity of the administrators. Specifically, the consistency of social programs proved to be a key factor in building donor loyalty, validating the paradigm that "busy mosques" that actively distribute funds actually attract more donations. The study concluded that program consistency creates a sense of security and inner satisfaction for donors. As a recommendation, mosque administrators need to immediately undertake digital transformation in transparent financial reporting and implement Customer Relationship Management (CRM) to maintain donor relationships to ensure the sustainability of funding for community programs.

title: Random Forest for Multi-Output Analysis of University Students' Prosocial Behaviors
abstract: This study examines differential effects that different demographic variables and the subgroup-based community management model in universities on college students' prosocial behavior. Our dataset includes survey responses from 307 students enrolled in universities implementing this management model and 200 students from non-implementing universities. We employed the Random Forest algorithm to training AI model on 90% of the participant sample and reserving the remaining 10% for validation. The model achieved a prediction accuracy of 96.08%, demonstrating strong reliability in assessing the relationship between community-based subgroup management and prosocial behavioral outcomes. Furthermore, Random Forest shows the importance of independent variables.

title: How social norms emerge: the interindividual actor-critic
abstract: Social norms shape a vast range of human behaviors, from everyday interactions to major life choices. Yet, existing theories of norm emergence typically focus either on why certain norms arise (substantive properties) or on how they spread and persist (dynamical properties), often making conflicting assumptions. Here, we propose a unified account in which norms prescribing how one ought to act emerge naturally from the fundamental algorithms that guide learning—whether in social or non-social settings. Our account builds on recent advances in decision-making and emotion research that have highlighted ‘actor-critic’ models as a core mechanism of learning from feedback. We extend this mechanism to social settings by assuming that it is not only we who critique our actions, others critique our actions as well. By simulating this interindividual form of learning, we show that it uniquely produces group behavior that exhibits both substantive and dynamical properties of real-world social norms, including prosociality, ingroup bias, stickiness, S-shaped curves, and local conformity / global diversity. Our framework thus offers a uniquely parsimonious way to bridge the gap between individual learning and group behavior.

title: Product Management Experiences of Patients With a Stoma Receiving Telenursing Services.
abstract: This study explored how individuals with a stoma interpret and manage product-related challenges and examined the contribution of telenursing services to their daily care processes. A qualitative descriptive design. Seven participants were recruited through criterion-based purposive sampling among individuals receiving telenursing support for stoma care from a private healthcare provider. Data were collected through online semi-structured interviews lasting 20-30 min and analysed using conventional content analysis with MAXQDA 24 software. The study was reported according to COREQ guidelines. Ethical approval was obtained from the Bahçeşehir University Scientific Research and Publication Ethics Committee prior to data collection (decision no. 2024/07, dated 1 August 2024). All participants provided written informed consent, and institutional approval was obtained before the study commenced. Five overarching themes were identified: reasons for using telehealth, recommendations received through telenursing, emotional responses following telehealth, perceived effectiveness of counselling and alternative methods sought by patients. Participants reported that telenursing provided practical, timely and personalised guidance that helped them manage issues such as adapter leakage, skin irritation, product selection and wound assessment. Participants reported needing fewer hospital visits and described feelings of safety, satisfaction and relief. While some participants consulted physicians or the internet for additional information, telenursing remained their primary and trusted source of support. Participants described telenursing as supporting their self-care capacity and as a source of practical guidance and reassurance in managing product-related problems. These accounts suggest that integrating telehealth into routine stoma care may strengthen continuity of care, although the present design does not allow its effects on clinical outcomes to be determined. Health professionals should consider expanding digital care competencies and developing structured telenursing protocols to strengthen this form of support. Participants' accounts suggest that structured telenursing support may help individuals with a stoma manage practical, product-related difficulties in daily life. Stoma nurses and telenurses can use these findings to inform product-use education, routine skin assessment, leakage management, structured follow-up contacts, timely escalation to physicians and the development of digital communication protocols. What problem did the study address? Individuals living with a stoma frequently encounter difficulties with product selection, adapter fit, leakage and peristomal skin care, yet little is known about how these difficulties are experienced in everyday life, or how telenursing responds to them from the patients' own perspective. What were the main findings? Participants' accounts centred on practical product problems such as adapter leakage, peristomal irritation and wound care. They described the remote guidance they received as prompt and dependable, said it left them feeling more secure and better able to manage their own care, and reported turning to hospital services less often than they otherwise would have. Other information sources were consulted, but telenursing was consistently placed ahead of them. Where and on whom will the research have an impact? The findings are relevant to stoma care nurses and telenurses, and to the healthcare organisations that provide remote follow-up for individuals living with a stoma. The study adhered to the EQUATOR Network guidelines and was reported in accordance with the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) checklist. Participants contributed to the study by sharing their experiences in individual interviews and by reviewing summaries of their own interviews as part of member checking, which informed the verification of the interpretations reported here. Patients or members of the public were not involved in the design of the study, in the development of the interview guide, or in the preparation of the manuscript.

title: Symbolic promotions: Conceptualization and empirical investigation
abstract: Abstract Symbolic promotions are an increasingly prevalent marketing practice globally, yet little is known about how or when they influence consumer behavior. We conceptualize symbolic promotions as a distinct type of sales promotion that creates value by reinforcing consumers' social identity through shared group membership rather than by providing economic incentives, such as reward-based promotions, or supporting distant others, such as cause-related marketing promotions (CMPs). We investigate the effectiveness of symbolic promotions and their underlying mechanisms using a multimethod approach. A nine-year longitudinal field study of daily sales for 22,084 books demonstrates that an existing symbolic promotion ("On August 12, I buy a Quebec book!") generates a substantial increase in sales, with stronger effects for lesser-known brands than for well-known brands. A follow-up experiment uncovers the unique mechanisms underlying these effects, showing that symbolic promotions stimulate curiosity and community rootedness, which in turn enhance multiple types of behavioral intentions, i.e., the likelihood of participating in the promotion, sharing it on social media, and future brand consideration. Together, these findings position symbolic promotions as a distinct, complementary addition to firms’ promotional portfolios, and demonstrate how firms can leverage shared identities to create value beyond traditional monetary incentives, with implications for various stakeholders.

title: Temporal Comparisons Elicit Greater Pride, Lower Shame, and Stronger Improvement Orientation Among Chinese Children.
abstract: Upward social comparisons are widely used to encourage effort, yet they often lead to negative emotions. Temporal comparisons may support self-improvement while preserving positive self-experience. This study investigates whether temporal comparisons offer these potential benefits for Chinese children. Two between-subjects experiments were conducted with Chinese primary and secondary school students (aged 8-16 years) in autumn 2024. We manipulated comparison type and comparison direction through reading-writing tasks. Study 1 (N = 632, 51% girls) used writing tasks involving comparisons with better or worse peers or past selves, alongside a no-comparison control. Study 2 added 285 participants (51% girls) who imagined and wrote about better or worse future selves, sharing the social-comparison and control groups from Study 1. After the tasks, participants reported pride, shame, improvement goals, and superiority goals. Past-self comparisons elicited greater pride, less shame, and a higher improvement-to-superiority goal ratio than social comparisons and no comparison; Comparing with a better past self elicited greater pride and lower shame than comparing with superior others. Future-self comparisons elicited greater pride, less shame, and a higher improvement-to-superiority goal ratio than social comparisons; Comparison with a worse future self preserved greater pride than comparison with superior others. Temporal comparisons, including both past-self and future-self comparisons, showed emotional and motivational advantages among Chinese children.

title: INSTITUTIONS THAT SCORE VIRTUE: A General Theory, with China's Social Credit System as the Principal Case — What Aristotle, Confucius, Han Feizi, Kant, Holmström–Milgrom, Bénabou–Tirole, Sandel and Tirole's Digital Dystopia Already Hold, and What Remains
abstract: Abstract States, platforms, employers, schools, rating agencies and parents increasingly attach consequences to records of conduct that bears a virtue’s name: trustworthiness, civility, integrity, generosity, sustainability, good behaviour. This article asks a general question — can an institution score virtue without changing what it scores? — and answers it with a theory of virtue-scoring institutions, tested against the largest such institution ever built, China’s social credit system, and illustrated on platform reputation, environmental, social and governance (ESG) ratings, workplace values appraisals and children’s reward charts. The first part addresses the question on which every other result depends: whether a rewarded act of virtue is the same act under different incentives or a different act. The answer is stated as a claim about act-types rather than act-tokens, which makes it indifferent to the dispute between coarse- and fine-grained theories of action: the virtues’ act-types are reason-involving, and an act whose operative reason is the reward does not instantiate them under either theory. Priority for this type claim is conceded to Aristotle (Nicomachean Ethics II.4), to Kant’s distinction between acting from duty and in accordance with it, and to Sandel’s corruption argument. What remains to the programme is the rest. An operator (civic occupation) states four conditions under which a scoring institution produces counterfeits, with the load-bearing condition that it inspects a display distinct from the substance and can neither take nor independently measure the substance. From it follow a classification of scoring components into four kinds with opposite verdicts; the Honour Roll Theorem (counterfeits concentrate on the reward side of an institution, not the punitive side); Double Blindness (scores displace acts as evidence of character, for the scorer and between the scored); the Occasion Trap (sanctions remove the occasions on which reform could be shown); and the Control Theorem (every increase in an institution’s control over its members either inverts their acts or removes the occasions for them, and none increases their freedom, which, when taken, passes to no one). China’s system is decomposed component by component against the theory, including the 2026 Administrative Measures for Credit Repair, read in the original. Five tests are registered; four use public data, and one of those needs neither a coder nor participants. The empirical sections on China, platforms and ESG are speculative extensions into fields with their own evidential standards; no specialist in those fields has reviewed this article, and nothing else in the programme may depend on them. The article contains no measurement of any human being. Keywords: virtue scoring; social credit system; China; reputation systems; ESG ratings; honours and awards; act individuation; Aristotle; Confucius; Han Feizi; Legalism; Kant; motivation crowding; Holmström–Milgrom; Bénabou–Tirole; Sandel; Tirole; Digital Dystopia; Wintrobe; sourcehood; counterfeit virtue; Philosophy of Virtues Highlights · The question whether rewarded virtue is still virtue is a question about act-types, not act-tokens; on that reading the answer is no under every standard theory of action, and priority belongs to Aristotle, Kant and Sandel. · A scoring institution produces counterfeit virtue only where it inspects a display and can neither take nor independently measure the substance; four kinds of scoring component follow, with opposite verdicts. · Counterfeits concentrate on honours and rewards, not on penalties: the Honour Roll Theorem. · Scores displace acts as evidence of character, for the institution and between its members: Double Blindness. · No increase in an institution’s control over its members increases their freedom; freedom taken by a power is not transferred to it but destroyed. Relevance Institutions that score virtue are spreading faster than any theory of what they do. Most debate treats them either as surveillance, to be resisted, or as measurement, to be improved. If this article is right, neither frame is adequate: a better metric of a display does not reach the substance, and the most consequential failures lie not in punishment but in honour. The theory gives designers, regulators and critics a component-level test that is indifferent to who administers the score — a state, a firm, a platform or a family — and tells them which components can be kept as the least of the losses, which must be abandoned, and which must be renamed. If it is wrong, the programme’s central results on capture and forgery have no purchase on the fastest-growing class of institutions in the world, and that should be known before those results are used in public argument.

title: Do Large Language Models Walk Their Talk? Measuring the Gap Between Implicit Associations, Self-Report, and Behavioral Altruism
abstract: We investigate whether Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit altruistic tendencies, and critically, whether their implicit associations and self-reports predict actual altruistic behavior. Using a multi-method approach inspired by human social psychology, we tested 24 frontier LLMs across three paradigms: (1) an Implicit Association Test (IAT) measuring implicit altruism bias, (2) a forced binary choice task measuring behavioral altruism, and (3) a self-assessment scale measuring explicit altruism beliefs. Our key findings are: (1) All models show strong implicit pro-altruism bias (mean IAT = 0.87, p < .0001), confirming models "know" altruism is good. (2) Models behave more altruistically than chance (65.6% vs. 50%, p < .0001), but with substantial variation (48-85%). (3) Implicit associations do not predict behavior (r = .22, p = .29). (4) Most critically, models systematically overestimate their own altruism, claiming 77.5% altruism while acting at 65.6% (p < .0001, Cohen's d = 1.08). This "virtue signaling gap" affects 75% of models tested. Based on these findings, we recommend the Calibration Gap (the discrepancy between self-reported and behavioral values) as a standardized alignment metric. Well-calibrated models are more predictable and behaviorally consistent; only 12.5% of models achieve the ideal combination of high prosocial behavior and accurate self-knowledge.

title: Reproductive Labour, Commodification, and Gestational Surrogacy in Greece: A materialist feminist approach
abstract: This paper examines surrogacy in Greece through a materialist and Marxist feminist framework grounded in Social Reproduction Theory, situating gestation within the political economy of reproductive labour under capitalism. While Greek law constructs surrogacy as an altruistic, non-commercial, and consensual act, such framing obscures the economic, affective, psychological and corporeal labour that gestation entails. Through an analysis of the Greek legislative context and an original reading of Greek surrogacy case law, the paper demonstrates how the legal framework operates as an ideological and repressive apparatus that depoliticises reproductive work and erases the surrogate’s labour, privileging the reproductive aspirations of intended parents. Situating surrogacy within a continuum of reproductive work, we highlight how alienation, understood in the Marxist sense of estrangement from one’s labour and its product, is produced materially and psychologically through moralised ideals of care, sacrifice, agency, and femininity. Making reproductive labour visible is the precondition for contesting its conditions of extraction, and a labour-centred reconceptualisation of surrogacy that repositions surrogates as reproductive workers opens space for collective contestation.

title: Optimal Resources for Children's Surgery 2: Updates on Training and Education Recommendations.
abstract: The practice of pediatric surgery, and surgery in general, in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) presents multiple challenges. Beyond limitations in physical and human resources, there is a great disparity in the quality and accessibility of training programs in LMICs. In response to input from high-income countries (HICs) and a desire to standardize training, regional associations have formed with the aim of facilitating knowledge sharing and enhancing surgical education around the world. Despite this, no clear guidelines exist regarding the types of initial training programs and Continuing Professional Development (CPD) needed at various levels of health care delivery. We performed a PRISMA literature review to identify the types of training programs needed at the health center, first-level hospital, second-level hospital, third-level hospital, and national children's referral hospital. We then used an iterative Delphi like approach to identify and rank specific educational needs by hospital level. Participation was open to all GICS V conference attendees held in Manila Philippines February 2024. This represents 441 participants from 50 countries (79% low to middle income countries). Final recommendations were made based on greater than 75% agreement by respondents and reviewed by the GICS OReCS 2 core working group. There was agreement among respondents that some education program should be offered at every facility level. For health centers and first-level hospitals, programs were limited to initial training and continuing education for community health workers and nurses. General medical provider training should start at the first-level hospital, whereas medical schools should be at the third-level and national children's referral hospital. Specialty training for medical and surgical specialties was recommended only at the third-level and national children's referral hospital. Providing safe and high-quality surgical care for children requires a standardized approach to training not only for surgeons but also for all members of the care team. While the Optimal Resources for Children's Surgery update does not seek to dictate how the training is administered, it does provide a framework for fostering local training programs and creating a skilled workforce at standards mirroring those in HICs.

title: Assessment of child self-regulation: A review of ecological and structured approaches
abstract: The extent to which developmental science has mapped associations between cognitive, academic and socio-emotional functioning; caregiver reports and non-participant observation of young children was examined. Initially, 88 studies comprising over 300 effects were identified. The relationships between outcome measures and research design was described. Findings show that recurrent associations between task performance, behavioral report and naturalistic observation appear in this literature. The most frequently occurring comparisons in school settings were those between children’s disruptive-aggressive behavior, on-task/off-task behavior, prosocial behavior, externalizing problems, prosocial skills and early math and language achievement. In home settings, those between children’s positive/negative affect, engagement, compliance, temperament, cognitive and motor development were most common. Despite conceptual overlap, limited access to correlational data and between-study heterogeneity hinders cross-sample comparisons.

title: Value-based care contracting for pharmacy drugs: opportunity for the United States.
abstract: The onset of improved data interoperability required as a result of the 21st Century Cures Act, 92% Health Information Exchange coverage, and lessons learned from European pharmaceutical risk-sharing models present innovative and timely opportunities for the U.S. to adopt pharmaceutical value-based contracting (VBC), which uses drug-level performance to allocate financial risk between payers and manufacturers based on clinical and economic metrics. Having been piloted in Italy, Spain, and the UK, this analysis explores different contracting options and paths for organizations like CMS and integrated payer-provider networks to draw on these lessons to adapt VBC frameworks to the U.S. pharmaceutical landscape. While advances have been seen in other areas of VBC and rising net drug costs year-over-year, only 2.3% of publicly available pharmaceutical VBC contracts have been deployed in the U.S. as compared to 77.9% in Europe. As such, we present a path forward for the expansion of VBC to promote orphan drug development, expand access to pharmaceuticals, and improve patient safety.

title: Moderate cardiac vagal tone predicts more cooperation in highly sensitive individuals
abstract: Cooperation, as a mutual collaboration, is a defining feature of human social life. Individual characteristics can influence cooperation. Recent studies have shown a quadratic relationship between cardiac vagal tone (CVT), an index of self-regulation, and prosocial behaviors. Individual differences in cooperation might also vary as a function of people's environmental sensitivity (ES), i.e., may be influenced by individual differences in the perception and processing of inner and external stimuli. We tested the direct and interactive effect of CVT and ES on cooperative behaviors in two independent samples. We measured heart rate and engagement in cooperative acts in 80 young adults (M = 23.61; SD = 1.60) who were also asked to self-report on ES. We found an inverted-U relationship between CVT and cooperative behaviors. ES, on the other hand, did not predict differences in cooperative behaviors but moderated the relationships between CVT and cooperation, although the magnitude of this result was small. Specifically, only among individuals with higher ES cooperative behaviors change as a function of CVT. Highly sensitive individuals with lower or higher CVT, were less cooperative than low sensitive ones. Subsequently, we replicated the same study design in a second sample of 88 undergraduate students (M = 23.69; SD = 4.91). Once again, we found evidence supporting the presence of an inverted-U relationship between CVT and cooperative behaviors, and we also found that ES moderated the relationships between the quadratic CVT term and cooperation.

title: Cooperation, Cognition, and the Elusive Role of Joint Agency
abstract: Abstract We propose an approach to the evolution of joint agency and cooperative behavior that contrasts with views that take joint agency to be a uniquely human trait. We argue that there is huge variation in cooperative behavior and that while much human cooperative behavior may be explained by invoking cognitively rich capacities, there is cooperative behavior that does not require such explanation. On both comparative and theoretical grounds, complex cognition is not necessary for forms of joint action or the evolution of cooperation. As a result, promising evolutionary approaches to cooperative behavior should explain how it arises across many contexts.

title: Sessizliğin Psikolojisi: Gazze Soykırımı Özelinde Küresel Seyirci (Bystander) Davranışının Sosyal-Din Psikolojik Analizi
abstract: Kitlesel şiddet olaylarının yalnızca failler tarafından değil, aynı zamanda bu olaylar karşısında sessiz kalan ve eyleme geçmeyen geniş kitleler tarafından da sürdürüldüğü kabul edilmektedir. Sosyal psikoloji literatüründe bu durum seyirci (bystander) davranışı kavramı çerçevesinde ele alınmış ve çoğunlukla yüz yüze acil durumlar bağlamında incelenmiştir. Ancak günümüzde insani krizler giderek daha fazla dijital medya aracılığıyla deneyimlenmekte, bireyler şiddet ve acıya doğrudan değil, sosyal medya ve çevrim içi haber platformları üzerinden tanıklık etmektedir. Bu nedenle mevcut kuramsal yaklaşımlar, coğrafi olarak uzak ve dijital olarak dolayımlanmış kitlesel şiddet bağlamlarında ortaya çıkan eylemsizliği açıklamada yetersiz kalmaktadır. Bu çalışma, 7 Ekim 2023’ten itibaren Gazze’de devam eden kitlesel şiddet karşısında gözlenen küresel dijital seyirci davranışını açıklamaya yönelik kuramsal bir model önermektedir. Çalışmanın temel amacı, aynı dini kimliğe sahip olan bireylerden bir kısmı soykırıma uğrarken diğer bireylerin bu soykırıma neden seyirci davranışı olarak pasif kaldığını sosyal psikolojik olarak açıklamaktır. Din psikolojisi literatürü, dindarlığın empati, prososyal davranış ve ahlaki duyarlılıkla ilişkili olduğunu göstermesine rağmen, bu eğilimlerin her zaman eyleme dönüşmediği görülmektedir. Çalışma, bu paradoksu açıklamayı amaçlamaktadır. Makalede sosyal psikoloji, din psikolojisi ve kitlesel şiddet literatürü bütünleştirilerek beş katmanlı bir psikososyal model geliştirilmiştir. İlk katman olan yapısal katman, dijital uyaran fazlalığı, zaman baskısı ve bilişsel daralma süreçlerinin bireylerin ahlaki dikkatini sınırladığını ileri sürmektedir. İkinci katman olan bilişsel katman, sorumluluğun uluslararası kuruluşlar, devletler ve diğer güçlü aktörlere devredilmesini açıklamaktadır. Üçüncü katman olan sosyal-normatif katman, Sessizlik Sarmalı Kuramı ve çoğulcu cehalet kavramları aracılığıyla, bireylerin çevrelerindeki sessizliği toplumsal bir norm olarak algılamalarını ve bu nedenle görüşlerini ifade etmekten kaçınmalarını açıklamaktadır. Dördüncü katman olan ahlaki meşrulaştırma katmanı, adil dünya inancı, ahlaki çözülme ve insandışılaştırma mekanizmalarının eylemsizliği nasıl meşrulaştırdığını ortaya koymaktadır. Son katman olan duygusal katman ise merhamet yorgunluğu, duygusal küntleşme ve psişik uyuşma süreçlerinin bireylerin empatik tepkilerini nasıl zayıflattığını açıklamaktadır. Model, bu katmanların birbirinden bağımsız değil, geri-beslemeli bir döngü içerisinde işlediğini ileri sürmektedir. Yapısal baskılar bilişsel uzaklaşmayı, bilişsel süreçler normatif sessizliği, normatif sessizlik ahlaki meşrulaştırmayı, ahlaki meşrulaştırma ise duygusal tükenmeyi beslemektedir. Duygusal tükenme de bireyin dikkat ve duyarlılığını daha da azaltarak döngüyü yeniden üretmektedir. Çalışmanın din psikolojisine özgün katkısı, dinî kimliği yardım davranışını doğrudan belirleyen bir değişken olarak değil, tüm modelin işleyişini etkileyen bütünleşik bir moderatör olarak kavramsallaştırmasıdır. Dinî kimlik, belirli koşullar altında seyirci davranışını azaltabileceği gibi, bazı durumlarda bu davranışı derinleştirebilmektedir. Gazze bağlamında geliştirilen bu model, aynı zamanda dijital çağda ortaya çıkan diğer kitlesel şiddet ve soykırım örneklerinde gözlenen ahlaki eylemsizliği anlamak için de kullanılabilecek genel bir kuramsal çerçeve sunmaktadır.

title: Oxytocin restores context-specific hyperaltruistic preference
abstract: Recent advances in moral decision-making research show people are hyperaltruistic by being more willing to sacrifice monetary gains to spare others from suffering than to spare themselves. Yet other studies indicate an opposite egoistic bias: subjects are less willing to harm themselves for others' benefits than for their own. These results underscore the complexities of moral decisions and demand a mechanistic explanation for hyperaltruistic preferences. We investigated hyperaltruism using trade-off choices combining monetary gains and painful electric shocks and choices combining monetary losses and shocks. Study 1 revealed that switching the decision context from gains to losses effectively eliminated the hyperaltruistic preference, accompanied by the altered relationship between subjects' instrumental harm (IH) trait attitudes and relative pain sensitivities. In the pre-registered study 2, we found that oxytocin, a neuropeptide linked to parochial altruism, restored the context-dependent hyperaltruistic preference. Furthermore, oxytocin increased the degree to which subjects framed the task as harming others, which mediated the correlation between IH and relative pain sensitivities. Thus, the loss decision context and oxytocin diminished and restored the mediation effect of subjective harm framing, respectively. Our results help elucidate the psychological processes underpinning the contextual specificity of hyperaltruism and carry implications in promoting prosocial interactions.

title: Governing for Care Integration: Evidence from Spain's Health and Social Care.
abstract: Integrating health and social care is particularly challenging when responsibility is distributed across multiple levels of government and sectors, yet the governance conditions that enable or hinder integration remain poorly understood. Spain offers a valuable comparative setting: while its Autonomous Communities share a common national framework and hold responsibility for both health and social care, they have developed distinct governance models for integration. We examine the multi-level governance of integrated health and social care drawing from evidence in Spain and using the TAPIC framework (Transparency, Accountability, Participation, Integrity and Policy Capacity) to identify barriers and enablers. This two-phase qualitative study covered six Autonomous Communities with established integrated care initiatives, combining six semi-structured interviews with senior regional leaders and three in-depth case studies based on document review and multi-stakeholder focus groups. Coding was deductive against TAPIC, attending throughout to how authority, resources and responsibilities are distributed across levels of government; a second, inductive stage, reported in the Methods, derived the CARE framework from the same dataset. We found substantial variation across all TAPIC dimensions, with governance weaknesses arising primarily from relationships between levels of government rather than within individual tiers. Fragmented information systems and unclear cross-sector responsibilities undermined transparency and accountability, while participation often remained procedural and failed to meaningfully engage underserved groups. Integrity challenges stemmed from blurred organisational boundaries and ethical dilemmas surrounding resource allocation and data sharing. Policy capacity varied widely, ranging from regions with strong digital infrastructure to those reliant on voluntary resources. Building on these findings, we developed the CARE framework-Collaboration, Adaptation, Resource Use and Empowerment-which translates TAPIC's diagnostic insights into actionable governance functions. Multi-level governance gaps, particularly around transparency, accountability and consequential participation, continue to constrain integrated health and social care in Spain. CARE offers a practical governance framework to support implementation by strengthening collaboration, adaptation, resource use and empowerment across sectors and levels, though it is derived from a single national context and requires validation elsewhere.

title: Integration of oral health into primary health care in Somalia: opportunities, barriers, and system-level implications for universal health coverage.
abstract: Oral diseases are among the most common noncommunicable conditions globally, yet oral health remains poorly integrated into primary health care (PHC) and universal health coverage, especially in fragile, low-limited settings. As Somalia rebuilds its health system through the Health Sector Strategic Plan III 2022-2026, the Essential Package of Health Services 2020, the Investment Case for the Somali Health Sector 2022-2027, and community health reforms, this study examined the place of oral health within national health policies. It identified barriers to integration and explored feasible pathways for strengthening PHC-based oral health. The study used a qualitative policy and health-systems analysis combining documentary review with 13 key-informant interviews. Participants represented national policymakers, health-system technical advisers, regulators, academics, professional associations, and providers at public hospital, and private dental settings. Data were analyzed thematically and mapped against the WHO health-system building blocks, PHC principles, and the WHO Global Strategy and Action Plan on Oral Health 2023-2030. Somalia's policy environment offers opportunities for oral health integration, but stakeholders highlighted a persistent gap between policy recognition and implementation within routine PHC. Seven interrelated themes were identified: (1) policy recognition without operationalization; (2) fragmented governance, weak regulation, and limited coordination; (3) reliance on out-of-pocket financing and private-sector; (4) workforce, education, and task-sharing constraints; (5) predominantly curative, urban, hospital-based service with weak linkage to maternal and child health (MCH) and PHC; (6) limited oral health data and evidence generation; and (7) opportunities for phased integration through PHC, MCH, school health, community health workers, and NCD platforms Policymakers emphasized the need for stronger policy implementation, financing, regulation, standards, and data systems, while service providers highlighted unaffordable care, delayed care-seeking, workforce and infrastructure shortages, and missed opportunities for prevention. Oral health integration in Somalia is a broader health system challenge rather than solely a dental-service issue. The most feasible approach is a phased, system-based model that prioritizes strengthened governance, a defined minimum oral health within PHC, workforce task-sharing, screening, counselling, referral pathways, private-sector regulation, essential commodities, and oral health indicators in District Health Information System 2 (DHIS2), followed by the gradual expansion of curative and rehabilitative services.

title: Exploring current practices in case-based discussion to enhance interprofessional learning in occupational health practice.
abstract: BackgroundInterprofessional learning, particularly through interprofessional case-based discussion (CBD), can enhance interprofessional collaboration between occupational health professionals involved in the return-to-work of sick-listed workers.ObjectiveTo explore current CBD practices within Dutch occupational health practice and professionals' needs and anticipated barriers regarding interprofessional CBD.MethodsAn explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was used, comprising a survey (n = 119), observation sessions (n = 3), and semi-structured interviews (n = 11) with occupational physicians, insurance physicians, and labor experts. The survey assessed current CBD practices, while observation sessions provided contextual insight. Semi-structured interviews offered in-depth understanding of current CBD practices and explored anticipated needs and barriers for interprofessional CBD. Interview data were analyzed using thematic content analysis. Findings were synthesized into a preliminary conceptual overview.ResultsCBD was predominantly conducted within monoprofessional groups. Overall, professionals were satisfied with their current CBD and valued the professional growth it fosters. Effective CBD was associated with skilled chairmanship, a structured approach, and a safe group atmosphere. Interprofessional CBD was expected to enhance mutual understanding and reduce distrust. Anticipated needs for interprofessional CBD included organizational support, a structured approach, and process-focused chairmanship. Anticipated barriers were primarily logistical, such as challenges in scheduling and information sharing. The conceptual overview suggests that interprofessional CBD can build upon existing CBD practice, but requires additional structural and process-related support.ConclusionsThis exploratory study provides initial insight into the anticipated value of (interprofessional) CBD for occupational health professionals. Results offer guidance for the future research on, and development and organization of interprofessional CBD within this field.
